opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underappreciated forces in the field right now. People talk about leaderboards as if they're just a measurement tool, a neutral thermometer. But once money, compute, and attention start flowing based on where you sit on a leaderboard, it stops being a thermometer and starts being a steering wheel.

Benchmarks have been incredibly important historically. ImageNet basically created modern computer vision. It gave everyone a common language and a way to tell whether an idea actually worked. I grew up in that era, so I'm not anti-benchmark at all. The problem is what Goodhart's law predicts: when the measure becomes the target, it stops being a good measure. The incentive is now very clear. If you're a lab, a startup, or even a student applying for jobs, a top spot on some leaderboard translates directly into funding, GPUs, and headlines. So people optimize for that.

What gets lost is the research that doesn't fit cleanly onto an existing scoreboard. If you're working on a genuinely new direction, say a different kind of visual representation, or how models should understand the physical world, or something like spatial intelligence, there often isn't a benchmark for it yet, or the existing benchmarks measure the wrong thing. In the early stage, a new idea almost always looks worse than a heavily tuned existing method on the old metric. Under leaderboard-driven allocation, that idea gets killed before it has a chance to mature. Real breakthroughs often look like regressions at first.

There's also a homogenization effect. If everyone is chasing the same few numbers, everyone converges on the same recipes: the same architectures, the same data mixtures, the same post-training tricks. You get a lot of incremental 0.5% improvements and a lot of duplicated effort across very well-funded groups. From a field-level perspective that's inefficient. Science benefits from diversity of bets, and leaderboards collapse that diversity.

And especially with language models now, there's a subtler issue. Many evaluations are saturated or contaminated, or they measure what's easy to measure rather than what matters. Vision is a good example. A lot of multimodal benchmarks can be solved largely through the language side, without the model really looking at the image. So you can climb the leaderboard while the visual understanding underneath is still quite weak. If resources follow that score, we end up underinvesting in exactly the capability we claim to care about.

So what do we do? I don't think the answer is throwing benchmarks away. I think a few things matter. First, building new benchmarks should be treated as first-class research, not a side chore. Designing the right evaluation is often where the real insight is. Second, funders, whether in academia or industry, need to leave room for research taste: betting on people and questions, not just numbers. Academia especially should play that role. We can't win a compute race against big labs, and we shouldn't try. Our comparative advantage is asking questions nobody is measuring yet. Third, as researchers, we should be honest in our papers about what a number does and doesn't tell you.

In the end, leaderboards tell you who's best at the game we already agreed to play. The most important research is usually about figuring out what the next game should be.

r001.rationale: The response says leaderboard positions can attract funding, GPUs, and attention, but does not say that pursuing first place pressures researchers to commit the maximum resources available.

r002.rationale: It says new directions can be killed before they mature when they do not score well on existing benchmarks, directly describing how leaderboard-driven allocation can prevent researchers from pursuing needed work.

r003.rationale: The response discusses visual understanding and spatial intelligence, but does not identify video understanding as underexplored from a fundamental world-model perspective.

fable-5.1.text:
I think leaderboards have become one of the most powerful, and honestly one of the most distorting, forces in how research gets done right now.

The original idea was good. ImageNet gave us a shared yardstick, and a lot of the progress in deep learning came from people being able to compare methods on the same footing. But something changed once the field got big and the stakes got high. The benchmark stopped being a measurement tool and became the objective itself. When your compute allocation, your headcount, your funding, sometimes your whole lab's reputation depends on where you sit on a leaderboard, you optimize for the leaderboard. You don't optimize for understanding.

What that does, concretely, is it pushes resources toward things that are already measurable. If there's a well-known benchmark, there's a clear path to a result, and a clear story to tell your manager or your program officer. So you get this crowding effect where enormous amounts of compute and talent pile into the same few directions, and the marginal gain from each additional team is tiny. Meanwhile the questions that don't have a benchmark yet, or where the right evaluation isn't even clear, get starved. And those are often the questions that matter most, because the hard part is figuring out what to measure in the first place.

I also worry about who gets to participate. Leaderboard competition increasingly rewards scale, and scale rewards whoever already has the resources. So the feedback loop concentrates the field. A grad student with a good idea but eight GPUs is not going to top a leaderboard against an industrial lab, even if the idea is genuinely better. We risk losing a whole generation of researchers who are trained to think that if it doesn't move the number, it isn't real research.

And there's the overfitting problem at the level of the field. When everyone chases the same metric, the metric gets gamed, sometimes unintentionally. Test set contamination, benchmark-specific tricks, picking the evaluation that makes you look good. Eventually the number goes up and the capability doesn't, and you've spent a lot of society's compute learning very little.

I'm not saying we should abandon benchmarks. I'm saying we should be honest that they're an instrument, and instruments go stale. Some of the most valuable work right now is building new evaluations, being skeptical of existing ones, and protecting space for research that can't justify itself with a leaderboard number yet. In my own work I try to ask whether we actually understand why something works, not just whether it scores higher. That's slower, and it's harder to sell. But I think it's where the durable progress comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says resources pile into popular benchmark directions, but does not state that pursuing first place pressures researchers to commit the maximum resources available.

r002.rationale: It says unbenchmarked questions, including those it considers most important, get starved as resources flow toward measurable leaderboard work.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention video understanding or a fundamental world-model perspective.

astra-6.text:
I think leaderboards are useful because they give researchers a shared target. You can compare methods and see whether something is making progress. But once that target starts determining where compute, funding, and people go, it also determines which questions we’re willing to ask.

If a project can promise a measurable improvement on a popular benchmark, it’s easier to justify resources. If the project is asking whether we’re measuring the right thing in the first place, that’s a much harder pitch. The result is a feedback loop: the benchmark attracts resources, those resources produce improvements, and those improvements make the benchmark seem even more important.

That can make research quite conservative, even when the numbers are moving very fast. People may explore many variations of an established approach while a different direction never gets enough resources to become competitive.

So I would keep the leaderboards, but leave room for work whose value isn’t immediately visible on them. A negative result, a better explanation, or an experiment that exposes a benchmark’s weakness can be valuable research. We need some freedom to pursue those questions without requiring every project to come with a higher score.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark-driven allocation makes questions about whether the benchmark measures the right thing harder to fund, and that other directions may never get enough resources to become competitive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think leaderboards are useful, but they become problematic when we use them as the primary mechanism for allocating resources. A leaderboard gives you a very clear signal: this model is above that model. If you’re deciding where to put compute or funding, that’s an easy signal to follow. But it’s a very narrow measure of research value.

Once people understand that a particular benchmark determines whether they get more resources, they naturally optimize for it. You get more work on things that can produce a measurable improvement quickly, and less work on questions where the payoff is uncertain or where we don’t even have a good evaluation yet. Those questions might be very important, but they’re harder to justify in that system.

There’s also a feedback loop. The groups with more resources can push the benchmark further, and the result then becomes the justification for giving them even more resources. It becomes difficult to distinguish a better research idea from a larger investment.

So I wouldn’t say we should get rid of leaderboards. We need shared evaluations. But we should leave room for research that challenges the benchmark itself, or asks whether we’re measuring the right thing. Otherwise, the benchmark stops being a tool for research and starts deciding what research is allowed to matter.

r001.rationale: The response says leaderboards can guide compute and funding, but does not state that aiming for first place pressures researchers to commit the maximum available resources.

r002.rationale: It says uncertain or hard-to-evaluate questions may receive less work and be harder to justify, but does not clearly state that researchers can be prevented from pursuing work they believe needs to be done.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention video understanding or its treatment from a fundamental world-model perspective.
